589.title: The sage
589.hook: the sage has no house to guard and no friendships built on fear
589.howItsDone: Buddhists call the Buddha Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas, especially in Mahayana traditions, and the ideal of the quiet, unattached sage runs through the oldest poems of the Sutta Nipata.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body poem, and your line, as it is. Did you pass a mirror without a verdict? Today, the last poem of the first chapter, and an old word for a wise person. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

Count the things you have to keep an eye on. Passwords. The car's next service. The plant that's dying. Subscriptions you forgot. Friends who'd be upset if you didn't reply by tonight. None of it is bad. But each one is a small hook, and some days you're mostly hooks. Two and a half thousand years ago, India had a word for a person who'd taken most of the hooks out. Not a priest, not a scholar. Someone quiet, wise, unattached, often wandering. The twelfth poem of the Sutta Nipata is about that person. Today's word: muni.
screen: `PASSWORDS, PLANTS, REPLIES.` → `SOME DAYS YOU'RE MOSTLY HOOKS.` → `A WORD FOR SOMEONE WITHOUT THEM.`

segments.voice: Muni means sage, a silent, wise one. The Buddha himself is often called Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakya people. The Muni Sutta opens with a strong line. From intimacy, fear is born. From a home, dust arises. To be without a home and without that kind of clinging: that's the sage's way of seeing. That sounds harsh until you hear the word underneath. Santhava, the intimacy here, means familiarity that binds, the closeness that makes you afraid of losing someone's approval. Fear-built friendships. The sage isn't cold. The sage has just stopped making friends out of fear. Then the poem gives pictures. The sage stands firm, like a post at a river's bathing place, while other people talk in extremes around it, praise and blame splashing on every side. The sage, it says, lives on what is given and doesn't flatter the giver or complain about the gift. And at the very end it adds a frank image: a blue-necked peacock never matches the speed of a swan in flight, and in the same way, the poem says, a householder doesn't match a sage meditating alone in the forest. That's the poem's view of the wandering life. Buddhist tradition as a whole also honors lay life, and many lay people are remembered as deeply wise. One more twist from the Dhammapada: nobody becomes a muni just by keeping silent. A fool can be quiet. The sage is the one who weighs things well and chooses the good.
screen: `MUNI: THE SILENT, WISE ONE` · `FROM FEAR-BUILT CLOSENESS, FEAR` · `A POST AT THE BATHING PLACE` · `NOT SILENCE: WEIGHING WELL` · then, large: `THE SAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live lightly today, and start by taking out one hook. Sit and settle. Notice one tie in your life that runs on fear: a reply you dread being late with, an approval you keep checking for. Don't cut the person off. Just loosen the fear. Breathe out and let the hook slip. Then picture the post at the river: people splash praise and blame, and it simply stands. Feel yourself as steady as that post for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Muni. A sage, a silent wise one: no house to guard, no friendships built on fear, steady as a post while praise and blame splash by. Today's word.
Your line: the sage. When you feel a fear-hook pull today, the urgent reply, the need to please, pause and stand like the post for one breath. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

590.title: The jewel discourse
590.hook: a city in crisis, and a verse chanted along its walls through the night
590.howItsDone: The Ratana Sutta is one of the most often chanted paritta, or protective texts, in Theravada Buddhism; monks chant it at blessings, for the sick, and in times of public crisis, often over a bowl of water that is then sprinkled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the muni, and your line, the sage. Did you stand like the post for one breath? Today, a new chapter of the Sutta Nipata begins, in a city in trouble. Day five hundred ninety.

Vesali was a rich, proud city, run by a council of nobles called the Licchavis. And then, the story goes, everything went wrong at once. The rains failed. Crops died. People starved, and sickness spread through the streets, and the city was full of dread. The council sent messengers south to Rajagaha to ask the Buddha to come. He came. And the tradition says that the moment he set foot in their territory, the sky opened and it poured. Then he gave Ananda a set of verses to carry through the city. Today: the jewel discourse.
screen: `VESALI: FAMINE AND SICKNESS.` → `MESSENGERS TO RAJAGAHA.` → `THE SKY OPENS.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Ratana Sutta, the discourse on the jewel. The story around it comes from the commentary: Ananda walked along the city walls all night, chanting the verses and sprinkling water from the Buddha's bowl, and the city recovered. The poem itself starts by speaking to every being gathered there, visible or not: may all of you be happy, and listen. Show kindness to the humans who bring you offerings day and night, and protect them. Then come the verses that give it its name. Whatever treasure there is in this world or any other, nothing equals the one who has fully awakened. Then a line that ends verse after verse, like a bell. In Pali: etena saccena suvatthi hotu. By this truth, may there be well-being. It's called an act of truth. In old India, people believed that stating something deeply true, solemnly, has power. So the poem states truths: the Buddha is a jewel, the teaching is a jewel, the community of noble disciples is a jewel. And on each truth, it rests a wish for safety. One verse near the end is especially loved. The old is used up, nothing new arises; the wise go out, the poem says, like this lamp. Picture Ananda saying that at night, perhaps holding a flame. Today, monks in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar and beyond still chant this poem when a home is blessed, when someone is sick, and when whole countries are frightened.
screen: `ANANDA WALKS THE WALLS AT NIGHT` · `MAY ALL BEINGS HERE BE HAPPY` · `BY THIS TRUTH, MAY THERE BE WELL-BEING` · `THE WISE GO OUT LIKE THIS LAMP` · then, large: `THE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: chant one verse for protection, or listen to it inside. Sit and settle. Think of a person or a place that needs safety right now. If you chant, say the Pali refrain slowly, three times: etena saccena suvatthi hotu. If you'd rather, just hold its meaning: by this truth, may there be well-being. Let the words rest on that person or place, like water sprinkled gently. Then sit in quiet, the way a city sleeps after rain. The bell holds the time.
The jewel discourse. The Ratana Sutta: truths about the Buddha, the teaching and the community, each one ending with a wish for well-being, chanted in times of fear. Today's word.
Your line: the jewel. When you hear bad news today, near or far, pause for one breath and wish that place well-being. Day five hundred ninety.

what it means: it's an act of truth: stating what is deeply true, and resting a wish for safety on it.

591.title: The smell of deeds
591.hook: a strict ascetic asks a buddha about the smell of raw flesh, and gets a list of deeds
591.howItsDone: Theravada monastics accept the food lay people offer, including meat not killed for them, while many Mahayana monasteries and lay Buddhists, especially in China, Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, keep a vegetarian diet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the jewel discourse, and your line, the jewel. Did you wish a troubled place well-being? Today, an argument about dinner. Day five hundred ninety-one.

Some people have strong views about what's on your plate. Sometimes it's you. And food rules are serious things: they shape families, holidays, whole communities. The second poem of the second chapter is an argument about food, and it's set long before the Buddha we know. It's told about Kassapa, a buddha the tradition says lived in an earlier age. An ascetic named Tissa, who eats only wild grain, beans, leaves and fruit, sees him accept a meal with meat in it. And Tissa challenges him. Today: the smell of deeds.
screen: `WHAT'S ON YOUR PLATE?` → `A BUDDHA OF AN EARLIER AGE.` → `AN ASCETIC'S CHALLENGE.`

segments.voice: Tissa's word is amagandha. Ama means raw, gandha means smell. The smell of raw flesh: in his world, a word for what is impure, rotten. The good ones, he says, live on what grows wild, honestly gathered. But you eat fine dishes cooked by others, rice with the meat of birds, and still you say the rotten smell doesn't touch you. So what do you mean by it? Kassapa's answer is a list, and the list is the point. Killing, beating, cutting, tying up. Stealing. Lying. Cheating, fraud, empty learning. Going after another's partner. People who are harsh, cruel, backbiting, betraying friends, heartless, stingy. Anger, pride, stubbornness, hypocrisy, envy, boasting, arrogance. This, he says, is the rotten smell, not the eating of meat. Fasting, going naked, shaving the head, offerings and rites, none of them cleans a person who hasn't let go of doubt. The rot is in deeds. Tissa hears it, bows, and asks to join. The poem says that after the Buddha we know told this story again and again, others understood too. A plain word about Buddhists and food today, because traditions differ. Theravada monks and nuns eat what is offered, including meat, unless they saw, heard or suspect the animal was killed for them. Many Mahayana communities, especially in East Asia, keep a vegetarian diet, drawing on later scriptures. Both take this poem seriously. Both agree with Kassapa that cruelty and lying smell worse than any meal.
screen: `AMAGANDHA: THE SMELL OF RAW FLESH` · `KILLING, LYING, CHEATING, CRUELTY` · `THE ROT IS IN DEEDS` · `BUDDHISTS TODAY EAT DIFFERENTLY` · then, large: `THE SMELL OF DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one rotten deed, gently. Sit and settle. Look back over the last day or two. Was there a moment that, if deeds had a smell, would have smelled a little off? A sharp word. A small lie. A bit of gossip. Don't spiral. Just find it, name it plainly, and notice how it feels in the body. Then breathe out, and picture opening a window. Decide on one small way to clear the air. The bell holds the time.
The smell of deeds. Kassapa's answer to Tissa: the real rot isn't in the food, it's in cruelty, lies and pride. Today's word.
Your line: the smell of deeds. Open the window today: make the small repair, the apology or the honest correction, for the deed you caught. Day five hundred ninety-one.

what it means: it answers a real food debate: the impurity that matters is cruelty and dishonesty, not what's on the plate.

592.title: A real friend
592.hook: a friend isn't the one who says 'I'm your friend'; it's the one who stands by you
592.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often pair the Hiri Sutta with the advice to Sigala on true and false friends, and lay Buddhists in many countries learn these lists as practical guidance for friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tissa and Kassapa, and your line, the smell of deeds. Did you open the window on one? Today, a short poem about friendship that fits on an index card. Day five hundred ninety-two.

You're moving apartments. Forty boxes, a couch, a Saturday in August. In the group chat, a dozen people said, of course, anything you need! At eight in the morning, two of them show up. You will remember those two for the rest of your life. A few weeks ago, in the advice to Sigala, we heard how to tell true friends from false ones. The third poem of this chapter is shorter and sharper, five verses about the gap between saying and doing. Today: a real friend.
screen: `FORTY BOXES AND A COUCH.` → `A DOZEN SAID YES. TWO CAME.` → `SAYING AND DOING.`

segments.voice: The poem is called the Hiri Sutta, after the word it begins with: hiri, a sense of shame, a conscience. It starts with someone who has none, who says I'm your friend, but never takes on any task they could easily do. Know them, the poem says: they're not my friend. Then: someone who speaks pleasant words to friends but doesn't follow through. The wise see that person clearly: all talk, no doing. Then a surprise. It's also not a friend who is always on alert for a break, watching you for faults, keeping score. Friendship that's suspicious is its own kind of failure. And then the picture of the real thing. A real friend is the one you can rest on, the poem says, like a child asleep on a parent's chest. Someone others can't split you away from. Think about that image. A child on a parent's chest doesn't check, doesn't wonder whether it's safe, doesn't earn its place. It just rests. That's what being a real friend makes possible for someone else. And it's built by deeds, not speeches: showing up, doing the task you could do, not keeping a list of the other person's mistakes. The poem's last verses turn inward, to the quiet joy of a good life and of the teaching. As if to say: the kind of person who can be that friend is someone at peace enough not to need the credit.
screen: `I'M YOUR FRIEND, BUT NO HELP` · `ALL TALK, NO DOING` · `NOT ALWAYS WATCHING FOR FAULTS` · `A CHILD ASLEEP ON A PARENT'S CHEST` · then, large: `A REAL FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be that friend, starting with one name. Sit and settle. Think of someone in your life who could use a friend to rest on right now. Someone moving, grieving, overwhelmed, or just quiet lately. Picture what would actually help, not a message saying let me know if you need anything, but one specific task you could do. Drop off food. Fix the thing. Sit with them. Choose it. Then let go of any score-keeping you've been doing with them, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
A real friend. Not the one who says I'm your friend, but the one who does the task, doesn't keep score, and can be rested on like a parent's chest. Today's word.
Your line: a real friend. Do the one specific thing you chose for that person, today or this week, without announcing it first. Day five hundred ninety-two.

what a scholar hears: the Hiri Sutta (Sn 2.3) opens with hiri, conscience, and its image of resting like a son on the chest (urasiva putto) is one of the warmest pictures of friendship in the early texts.

593.title: The highest blessings
593.hook: the gods ask what truly brings good fortune; the first answer is about company
593.howItsDone: The Mangala Sutta is among the most widely chanted protective texts in Theravada Buddhism; it is recited at weddings, house blessings and new beginnings, and many children learn it by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the friend you can rest on, and your line, a real friend. Did you pick your one specific task? Today begins a poem we'll stay with for four days. Day five hundred ninety-three.

Lucky socks on game day. Knocking on wood. Not walking under a ladder. A lucky number on the apartment door. Every culture has its signs of good fortune, and the Buddha's India had plenty. The commentary tells a story: people argued for years about what was truly auspicious. Was it something you see, like a bird or a pot of water? Something you hear, a good word on waking? Something you touch? The argument spread, the story says, all the way up to the gods. So one night a god came down to the Jeta Grove to ask the Buddha. Today's word: mangala.
screen: `LUCKY SOCKS. KNOCK ON WOOD.` → `WHAT IS TRULY AUSPICIOUS?` → `A GOD COMES TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Mangala means blessing, good fortune, an auspicious sign. The poem is the Mangala Sutta, and it opens with the visitor's question: many gods and humans have thought about blessings, longing for well-being. Tell us the highest. Notice what the Buddha doesn't do. He doesn't say omens are silly. He just answers with a different kind of sign, one you can see in a life. Not keeping company with fools. Keeping company with the wise. Honoring those who deserve honor. That's the highest blessing, he says. That's the first verse. Your life starts with who you sit next to. Then the next verse: living in a good place, having done good in the past, setting yourself on the right course. Then: much learning, a skill or craft, being well trained, and speech that is well spoken. That's the highest blessing. The poem keeps going, verse after verse, and the tradition counts thirty-eight blessings in all. Each verse ends with the same line, which works like a stamp: this is the highest blessing. Here's what makes it different from lucky socks. An omen happens to you. These blessings are things you can do. Choose your company. Learn something well. Speak well. Fortune, in this poem, isn't waiting outside your door. It's built into how you live. Tomorrow, the poem comes home: to parents, family and work.
screen: `WHAT IS THE HIGHEST BLESSING?` · `NOT FOOLS: THE WISE` · `A GOOD PLACE, LEARNING, A SKILL` · `FORTUNE YOU CAN DO` · then, large: `THE HIGHEST BLESSINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep wise company, starting with a look at who you keep. Sit and settle. Bring to mind the people you spend the most time with, in person and on your screen. Who leaves you a little wiser, kinder, steadier? Who leaves you a little worse? No judgment, just noticing. Then choose one wise person you'd like to spend more time with, or one voice you could follow more, or one feed you could follow less. Hold that choice for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Mangala. A blessing, good fortune: and in the Buddha's answer, not an omen but a way of living, starting with wise company. Today's word.
Your line: the highest blessings. Spend ten minutes today with someone, or something, that makes you wiser. Day five hundred ninety-three.

594.title: Blessings at home
594.hook: the blessings poem walks into the house: parents, family, and work that isn't chaos
594.howItsDone: In many Buddhist families, caring for aging parents is seen as a central duty and a source of merit, and the Mangala Sutta's verses on family are chanted at weddings and house blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mangala, and your line, the highest blessings. Did you spend ten minutes in wise company? Today the same poem comes in through the front door. Day five hundred ninety-four.

A grandmother's hands, shelling peas at a kitchen table. A dad checking the lock twice before bed. Somebody picking up a parent's prescription on the way home from a long shift. None of it gets posted. None of it looks like a spiritual life. And yet the Buddha, asked by a god what the highest blessings are, gets to this exact scene by the fifth verse. Before meditation, before the deep teachings, the poem stops at home. Today: blessings at home.
screen: `SHELLING PEAS. CHECKING THE LOCK.` → `NOTHING ANYONE POSTS.` → `THE POEM STOPS AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Supporting your mother and father. Caring for your partner and your children. Work that is peaceful, not tangled and chaotic. That is the highest blessing. The text, from its time, says wife and children; many teachers today read it as whoever makes up your household. Notice the three. Looking up the generations, to parents. Looking across and down, to partner and children. And the work that feeds them all, done without turmoil. In the Buddha's teaching, caring for parents isn't a small duty. Elsewhere he says that even carrying your parents on your shoulders for a hundred years wouldn't repay them, though helping them toward goodness and wisdom does. Then the next verse widens the circle. Giving. Living by what is right. Helping your relatives. Actions no one could fault. That is the highest blessing. And the next. Keeping away from wrongdoing. Holding back from intoxicants. Being steady and careful in what is good. Listen to how ordinary this is. Pay the bills honestly. Call your aunt. Don't drink yourself into a mess. Take care of the people who took care of you. The poem doesn't say these lead to the blessings. It says they are the blessings. A tidy, peaceful home, a parent fed, a cousin helped: these are not the waiting room of the spiritual life. In this poem, they're inside it.
screen: `MOTHER, FATHER, PARTNER, CHILDREN` · `WORK THAT ISN'T CHAOS` · `GIVING, HELPING RELATIVES` · `NOT THE WAITING ROOM: THE THING ITSELF` · then, large: `A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for family today, starting with one picture. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone in your household or family: a parent, a partner, a child, a sibling, a cousin. If family is complicated for you, choose the person who has been family to you. See them doing something ordinary. Let a little gratitude rise. Then ask: what's one small act of care I could do for them today? A call, a meal, a chore done before they ask. Choose it. Then rest. The bell holds the time.

Blessings at home. In the Mangala Sutta: supporting parents, caring for partner and children, peaceful work, giving and helping relatives. Not steps toward the blessing: the blessing itself. Today's word.
Your line: a blessing. Do your one small act of care today, and when you do it, quietly call it what the poem calls it: a blessing. Day five hundred ninety-four.

595.title: Blessings of the heart
595.hook: respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, and being easy to correct
595.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice gratitude through daily chanting, offerings to monastics and teachers, and merit-dedication ceremonies for parents and ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the blessings at home, and your line, a blessing. Did you do your small act of care? Today ends the week, and the poem turns inward. Day five hundred ninety-five.

Someone at work points out a mistake in your report. Not cruelly; it's just wrong. And there's a tiny moment, maybe half a second, before you answer. In that half second, everything is decided. Do you bristle, explain, defend? Or do you say: oh, you're right, thanks? Most of us know which answer we'd like to give. The Mangala Sutta has a word for the second answer, and it calls it one of the highest blessings. So far the poem has covered company, learning, home and work. Now it reaches the qualities inside a person. Today: blessings of the heart.
screen: `A MISTAKE IN YOUR REPORT.` → `HALF A SECOND TO ANSWER.` → `THE POEM TURNS INWARD.`

segments.voice: The verse goes: respect and humility, contentment and gratitude, and hearing the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Then the next: patience, being easy to correct, seeing those who live a holy life, and talking about the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Look at gratitude. The Pali is kataññuta. Kata, what was done; ññu, knowing. Gratitude is knowing what has been done for you. Not a feeling you have to manufacture. A kind of seeing: someone made this meal, someone taught me to read, someone kept the lights on. The Buddha elsewhere says that grateful people, those who know what has been done for them, are rare in the world. And look at being easy to correct, sovacassata. Literally, being good to speak to. The person you can tell something to without a fight. It sits right next to patience, and it's the half-second answer from the report. These are blessings because they open a person. Contentment leaves room. Humility lets teaching in. Gratitude lets you see. This whole week has been about what's inside. The sage with no fear-built ties. The jewel, chanted on a truth. The smell of deeds, not of food. A friend you can rest on. Then wise company, home, and now the heart. It's the same poem's lesson: the good things in a life are mostly built from the inside out.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gratitude as seeing. Sit and settle. Look at one thing near you: a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing. Now trace what was done for it to be here. Someone grew the cotton, someone sewed, someone drove the truck, someone stocked the shelf. Don't force a warm feeling. Just know what was done. Then let one person who did something for you come to mind, and know that too. Rest in that knowing. The bell holds the time.
Blessings of the heart. In the Mangala Sutta: respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, patience and being easy to correct, the blessings that open a person. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude is a blessing. Tell one person today exactly what they did for you, not just thanks, but the thing itself. Day five hundred ninety-five.
